title: A Systematic Literature Review of Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM-Integrated Systems
explain_beginner: This paper looks at how attackers can trick AI systems that use large language models. The problem is that these models cannot tell the difference between real instructions and sneaky text hidden in content they read. The authors reviewed 81 studies and sorted them using a standard security framework. They found that most research focuses on the first point of contact, the prompt, and on two common attack goals. Other parts of real AI systems, like tools and memory, get far less attention. This matters because real systems have many parts, so gaps in research leave real gaps in protection.
explain_business: This review shows that current security research on AI prompt injection is heavily focused on one part of the system, the prompt, while other components like tools and memory are largely ignored. For executives, this means that published defences and threat models may not cover the full attack surface of production AI systems. The decision this informs is where to direct security investment and internal testing. Relying only on prompt-level protections is likely insufficient. Organisations deploying tool-augmented or memory-enabled AI should commission their own assessments of those less-studied boundaries and treat prompt injection as a system-level risk, not just a model-level flaw.
explain_practitioner: The authors conducted a PRISMA systematic review, searching IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, and ScienceDirect for peer-reviewed work from 2015 to October 2025. They included 89 publications and analysed 81. Each paper was coded against MITRE ATLAS version 5.4.0 along three axes: trust boundary, attacker objective, and research orientation. Attacker objectives were mapped to seventeen operational patterns. Results show a strong concentration on the prompt interface and on Instruction Hijack and Policy Bypass objectives. Tool and memory boundaries lack both attack characterisation and defence proposals. The authors attribute this to incentives favouring reproducible prompt-level experiments over complex architectural assessments.
